rationale: A wins because it is the adult in the room: it builds stories from the supplied facts and turns missing data into gates, not garnish. The A headline "Warby Parker says store shoppers spend more than online buyers. It will not say how much." is a real reporter question with a proof path. B has sharp instincts, but "What 40 chain optometry clinics mean for the independent eye doctor down the street" starts writing the consolidation story before the facts earn it.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker built its brand on skipping the middleman" is plausible company-history color, but it is not in the supplied update; keep it only if verified.

"That is the one metric in the update, and it is the reason the whole expansion exists" overstates causality; the update says Warby says retail customers spend more, not that this single metric drove the 40-store plan.
The pharmacy angle says the pilot "puts pressure on whoever currently sells eyewear in pharmacies and on incumbent optical chains"; that competitive impact is not supplied and needs market evidence.
gaps_in_B: "the shift of routine vision care out of independent optometry practices and into national retail chains" is an invented trend from this record; the update only gives Warby's own expansion.
"The DTC brand that proved you don't need stores now has 300 of them" builds a whole thesis-reversal angle on Warby history not provided in the update.

"What 40 chain optometry clinics mean for the independent eye doctor down the street" over-labels the stores as clinics and smuggles in a consolidation/workforce story without locations, hiring numbers, or market-impact proof.
"corporate-practice-of-optometry rules" may be a real issue, but no regulatory fact was supplied; B should flag it as a verification need, not let it steer the angle.
